title: The National Security Act and the NSC, 1947-1985
notes: nsam-303 belongs as the correction: a two-sentence renaming memo, not a charter.

lead.text: The National Security Act of 1947 created the National Security Council and placed the Central Intelligence Agency under it, and a residual clause in that Act, section 102(d)(5), is the authority the first covert-action charters were written under. This topic follows the Council's directive series from NSC 10/2 in 1948 to NSDD 159 in 1985, and the people who held its first offices.

summary.text: Truman's directive of 22 January 1946 created the post of Director of Central Intelligence, to be designated by the President, and Sidney Souers held it first. The Act of 26 July 1947 then created the National Security Council, the Central Intelligence Agency under the Council, and the National Military Establishment.

Section 102(d)(5) lets the Agency perform such other functions related to intelligence as the Council may direct. NSC 10/2 of 18 June 1948 and NSC 5412 of 15 March 1954 both invoke it, so the covert-action programme rests on a residual clause in a reorganisation statute.

The charters define covert operations by deniability: operations planned so that any US Government responsibility is not evident to unauthorised persons and, if uncovered, can be plausibly disclaimed. NSC 10/2 created an Office of Special Projects inside the CIA to conduct them, and NSC 5412 superseded it six years later with the same test.

The series ran on through a renaming memo in 1964, Carter's intelligence order of 1978, which routed every special activity to the President through an NSC committee, and Reagan's NSDD 159 of 1985, which put all covert action policy inside a separate specially compartmented access system.

record.text: The 1946 directive formed a Central Intelligence Group under a Director of Central Intelligence who sat as a non-voting member of the National Intelligence Authority, barred any police, law enforcement or internal security functions, and made the Director responsible for fully protecting intelligence sources and methods.

Souers signed as Director of Central Intelligence within two weeks, held the post from 22 January to 10 June 1946, and was Executive Secretary of the National Security Council from August 1947 to January 1950, the civilian staff head the 1947 Act provides for at section 101(c).

At the Council's first meeting on 26 September 1947, with Souers as Executive Secretary and the Director of Central Intelligence among those present, the Council gave the Executive Secretary full powers over its funds and recorded that its affairs would be conducted with the utmost secrecy.

The Act also created the National Security Resources Board, the Departments of the Army, Navy and Air Force, the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Munitions Board. It did not create the Department of Defense: it established the National Military Establishment, renamed by the amendments of 10 August 1949.

The Council's statutory purpose is still to advise the President on integrating domestic, foreign and military policies relating to national security. Its 1947 members were the President, the Secretaries of State, Defense, Army, Navy and Air Force and the Chairman of the National Security Resources Board; the Director of Central Intelligence was never a statutory member, and today the Director of National Intelligence attends only if the President so designates. Its professional staff is capped at 200.

James Forrestal was Secretary of the Navy until September 1947 and the first Secretary of Defense from 17 September 1947 to 28 March 1949. The Act requires the Secretary of Defense to be appointed from civilian life and bars anyone on active duty as a regular commissioned officer within the previous ten years.
Roscoe Hillenkoetter headed the Central Intelligence Agency from May 1947 to October 1950, on a CIA-held clipping.

NSC 10/2 created the Office of Special Projects inside the CIA to plan and conduct covert operations. Its Chief reported directly to the Director of Central Intelligence, and the office was to operate independently of the Agency's other components. The name Office of Policy Coordination appears with Frank G. Wisner as Assistant Director for Policy Coordination from 1 September 1948.

NSC 5412 was transmitted by the Council's Executive Secretary, James S. Lay Jr., with a note that the President had approved it that day. It made the Director of Central Intelligence responsible for keeping covert operations consistent with foreign and military policy, superseded and rescinded NSC 10/2 and NSC 10/5, and made the Operations Coordinating Board the normal channel for coordinating support.

NSAM 303 of 2 June 1964, signed by McGeorge Bundy rather than the President, has two operative sentences: the Special Group 5412 would henceforth be known as the 303 Committee, and the change did not alter its composition, function or responsibility as authorised by NSC 5412/2. It contains no secrecy policy of any kind and no mention of unidentified aerial phenomena.

Truman created the Psychological Strategy Board by directive of 4 April 1951, reporting to the Council, with a Board of the Under Secretary of State, the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Director of Central Intelligence. Gordon Gray was its first Director; the directive gave him a claim on other departments for assistance and information but did not authorise the Board or the Director to perform any psychological operations.

Gray's other offices, from the Office of the Historian's list, were Secretary of the Army from 1949 to 1950, Assistant Secretary of Defense for International Security Affairs from 1955 to 1957, and Special Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs from 1958 to 1961. A 1955 newspaper series records that the University of North Carolina gravity institute had his approval before he retired as the university's president.

Nixon's EO 11652 of 1972 lodged monitoring of the classification system in the National Security Council, with an Interagency Classification Review Committee that took complaints from within or without the government.

Carter's EO 12036 of 1978 required the Special Coordination Committee to submit a recommendation, with all dissents, to the President on each special activity, defined as an activity abroad where the US role is not apparent or acknowledged publicly. It required the intelligence committees to be kept fully and currently informed while saying that was not a condition precedent, and built a four-part oversight structure. It contains no compartmentation provision.

NSDD 159, signed by Reagan in January 1985, ordered the national security adviser to establish a separate, specially compartmented control and access system at Top Secret for all covert action policy, with one designated focal point per agency, knowledge of policy, operations and support strictly compartmented from each other, and the minimum possible number of documents. The only record copies of approved Findings and Memoranda of Notification were to be held by one NSC officer.

The NSDD 159 original carried the instruction Declassify on Presidential Approval Only and a struck-through control line reading TOP SECRET/VEIL. Its first partial release, in 1987, was made under EO 12356, and the fuller Reagan Library release differs from it.

Later agencies were founded under the same Act: DoD Directive 5105.15 of 7 February 1958 established ARPA in the Office of the Secretary of Defense in accordance with the National Security Act of 1947 as amended, with Roy W. Johnson as first Director.

Charles Cabell was the Air Force's Director of Intelligence to 1953, the office he held while Project Blue Book was created, and Deputy Director of Central Intelligence from 1953; the CIA's chronology records his resignation on 27 December 1961. The Act had also created the Air Force, whose Project Blue Book logged 12,618 sightings from 1947 to 1969, 701 of them unidentified, before the Secretary of the Air Force ended it on 17 December 1969.

The agencies under the Council later touched the subject directly: the CIA's Office of Scientific Intelligence convened the Robertson Panel in January 1953, the CIA's own historian conceded the Agency's role included shaping public explanations for classified overflights, and ODNI's 2021 assessment put its inability to characterise most incidents down to limited and inconsistent reporting.

claimed.text: Hillenkoetter, after leaving the Agency, said publicly in 1960 that the unknown objects were operating under intelligent control, asked for a congressional investigation, and as a NICAP board member referred his conclusions to the Senate Space Committee.

On the Danny Jones Podcast in June 2026, Matthew Ehret said the Office of Policy Coordination staffed NICAP's leadership, that the National Enquirer's founder worked in it before founding the paper and that Richard Bissell headed it, and that Blue Book was launched under CIA Deputy Director Cabell, whom Kennedy fired.

On AREA52 Debriefed in January 2025, Chris Ramsay read a list describing Gray as managing Cold War information in a way that aligned with MJ-12's supposed need to control UFO narratives, and read John Lear's 1987 statement that General James V. Forestall jumped to his death and that his medical records are sealed. In April 2025 Jesse Michels said on the same show, prefacing it with doubt, that Forrestal heard a description of mutilated human and alien bodies shortly before his hospitalisation.

Jason Reza Jorjani said on the Danny Jones Podcast in 2024 that the Herald Tribune's gravity reporting dated from 1953 and quoted Martin's chief executive promising production within a few years on Manhattan Project funding.

The board infers that the federated intelligence community is itself a concealment resource, because an activity placed in the seam between two elements can be nobody's to report, and that the CIA's later overflight explanation amounts to admitting it let false explanations stand.

contested.text: NSC 5412 does not create the 5412 Committee, contrary to a widely repeated claim: no Special Group appears in its text, and the State Department's editorial note attributes the Special Group to NSC 5412/2 of 28 December 1955, which NSAM 303 itself cites as the authority.
NSAM 303 is routinely cited for things it does not say: it is a renaming memo signed by the national security adviser, with no classification, declassification or subject-matter rules in it.

Two common statements about the 1947 Act rest on less than they seem. It created the National Military Establishment, not the Department of Defense, and the Statutes at Large print only its approval date, so Truman's signature, universally reported, was not verified from a primary signing document.

The opened records contradict the podcast versions: the only officer of the covert-action office they name is Wisner, from September 1948, and nothing opened bears on NICAP or the Enquirer; Cabell was still the Air Force's intelligence chief when Blue Book began and resigned rather than being dismissed; no document connects the Psychological Strategy Board to UFOs; Forrestal could not have been a general, since the office required a civilian; and the Herald Tribune series dates from November 1955 and quotes a vice-president, comparing the time rather than the funding of the first atom bomb.
Michels named no document and no date for the Forrestal account, and nothing supporting it was opened.

NSDD 159's own compartment rules are not in either release: the special access procedures were to be issued under separate cover and were not located, and VEIL appears only as a struck-through marking, so it cannot be said to be the name of the compartment the directive creates.
Hillenkoetter's claims had a contemporary critic in the 1960 Enquirer editorial, and a text search of his FBI files found no mention of NICAP, flying saucers or 1960, though the scans are uneven.

questions: What did NSC 5412/2 of 28 December 1955 say, and who sat on the Special Group it created?
Where are the special access procedures NSDD 159 says were issued under separate cover, and was VEIL the name of its compartment or an existing handling caveat?
Does any primary record show who signed the National Security Act of 1947?
Does the Navy's 1949 board of investigation into Forrestal's death survive, and does it bear on the claim that his medical records are sealed?
Is there any record at all behind the MJ-12 attributions made to Souers and Gray?
What records of Findings and Memoranda of Notification survive from the single NSC custodian NSDD 159 created?
